text: When you start getting to the middle of the game (turn 5ish), try to think of the cost vs return of the plants you want. This cost is directly related to turn order as resources are cheapest for the first player to buy them. As ohmmmkay says - try to stay 'behind' as much as possible. Ask yourself about how many turns will it take you until you see a profit from a plant you wish to buy. Then ask yourself if you plan on keeping that plant for at least that many turns. If the answer is no, don't buy it. You should have an idea of what plants will make it to the end game by now (hint: At least powering 4-5 houses by itself). I usually only buy houses when I have the plant + resources to power them OR someone will be jumping in my area and grabbing the cheap connection costs from me. But, you should be buying the absolute cheapest houses in the early game as you can. By the end, the connection costs really don't matter. There is no way to 'block' someone from buying up to the required number of houses we've found. Even if all 4 people try, it has always been possible for the 5th to find a way out and buy. Our group has gotten pretty good at playing. The only problem is we never make it to step 3 anymore. That means we never get to buy from the future market, meaning some people can just get screwed by the plants that flip over. We've been winning by powering only 11-12 houses and buying up to 15 since one player will get lucky and buy a plant that powers 6 while the next one that flips over pushes the other 6 power plant back to the future market making it impossible for anyone to buy big enough plants to contend.
label: supported_recommendation

text: As far as co-op board games, some of my favorites: 1. Pandemic - great game, not really much like Arkham Horror except you have to travel over a map to stop things from getting too bad. 2. Shadows Over Camelot - fantastic game, lots of things going on at once 3. Battlestar Galactica - not much like AH, but it's a great challenge with lots of fun and variety to it. 4. Minion Hunter - you might like this, if you can find a copy of it. In it, you're trying to stop post-apocalyptic horrors from taking over the world, sort of like AH. Plays better with its expansion, but good luck on finding that. 5. Ghost Stories - this game is tough. The mechanics aren't really like AH, but if you like a game that will kick your ass, look no further. 6. Red November - clever little game that supports lots of players but is pretty lightweight fare. Plus a couple of semi-co-operative games you might like: 1. Descent - basically DnD-like dungeon crawling in board game form, one player plays the monsters and the rest play the heroic party challenging the dungeon. 2. Fury Of Dracula - great game where one player plays Dracula and the rest co-operate to bring him down. 3. Buffy The Vampire Slayer: The Boardgame - one player plays the bad guy and everyone else is Buffy and her gang. Whatever you think of the TV show, this is actually a great game with lots of replayability. The re-designer of Arkham Horror put out a game called Android about 6 months ago or so. It's a rich, complex, Blade Runner-esque murder mystery with some interesting mechanics. It's each player for themselves though. Personally, Arkham Horror always struck me as kind of an adventure game, so I lump it in with Runebound, Talisman, Warrior Knights, etc.. But none of those are co-operative. Arkham Horror really does sort of stand on its own, though. Of all those I mentioned, maybe Minion Hunter comes closest to it. But you'll be hard-pressed to find another game just like it.
label: supported_recommendation

text: I don't know about your games of Agricola, but my group generally tries not to take an action unless it benefits them a lot and is not totally screwing somebody over. And we generally try to make sure nobody has to take a begging card within reason. I think speek is getting at the fact there is no direct action. By taking one thing over another you are indirectly affecting their actions. In other games, your actions can directly affect other players. In zombies for instance you are actively competing with other players and can play cards directly on them to affect them. It might just be the feel of the game, that you aren't really having any meaningful affect on other players, Race for the Galaxy without takeovers, or Puerto Rico, or Ticket to Ride, or Carcassone. Unless you predict exactly what somebody else is doing, there is no way to purposefully affect their play because they are pretty much doing their own thing.

text: It used to be a very easy choice for me - the only FLGS in town had terrible service. They didn't greet you, didn't ask if you were looking for something, only said anything once you were at the counter ready to fork over cash for highly marked-up games. With sites like Thought Hammer providing free 3-day shipping on any orders over $100, the choice was simple. However, a new store has opened up and they are a lot friendlier and you can tell they love games too. The prices are a bit steep and their selection is much more limited due to having a small game front, but when I can I'd like to support them. They do some great things like hosting a family game night at a local coffee shop once every week. It's pretty much nerd-city there, the social cavemen come out, but I think it's terrific they are at least trying to promote the hobby. They deserve some support. To summarize, I think if you have a good FLGS - you should support them if at all possible. If you don't have the option at all, or your options are crappy, there's no shame in ordering online.
